title: When Deterministic Verifiers Produce No Paired Gain: A Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair for LLM Network Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0d...) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline successes = 240/240, guarded successes = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the prespecified shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could only change outcomes when the single shared candidate failed deterministic validation or a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run every shared candidate passed validation and repair_attempts = 0, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We report the preregistered design and mapping to archived analysis outputs, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis of the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent into device configurations that are safe to apply remains a central NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly propose multi‑step device change plans, but correctness requires respecting sequencing, dependency, and transient invariants not captured by token‑level fidelity metrics. Emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configs are executed on device images or simulators and deterministically scored—reveals semantic failure modes such as unsafe transient states and protected‑resource touches [1].

Generate–validate–repair (GVR) augments generation with a deterministic verifier and an automated repair routine intended to eliminate unsafe candidates before application [2,3]. Prior studies report promising repair coverage on syntactic and many semantic faults, but key open questions remain about (a) whether deterministic verifiers reduce unsafe application rates under distribution shift or adversarial prompts, and (b) which experimental contracts reliably expose a causal paired benefit for the verifier. This paper presents a fully preregistered paired experiment that measured the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The run completed as planned but produced a degenerate paired contrast because every shared initial candidate passed validation and no repairs occurred. We (1) document the executed estimand and its artifact mapping, (2) present the empirical outcome and statistical inference, and (3) provide an evidence‑grounded failure analysis and design recommendations so future experiments can produce informative paired contrasts.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents in network configuration evaluate end‑to‑end task execution rather than text fidelity alone; NetConfArena is a recent instantiation of this approach [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and program repair frames generate–validate patterns and demonstrates that validators often enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, with semantic coverage depending on verifier design and check sets [2,4]. Survey and position work synthesize verifier integration, tool augmentation, and uncertainty calibration as promising practices for operational NetOps automation, and engineering precedents such as Batfish illustrate verifier design tradeoffs [3,5,6].

Our study differs from these prior works by (a) preregistering a single, precisely defined paired estimand, (b) executing under shared_initial_candidate semantics so both arms start from the identical initial LLM candidate, (c) using deterministic emulator scoring to determine safe vs unsafe application, and (d) archiving per‑call traces and analysis artifacts so the exact measured estimand is reconcilable to the execution bundle.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0d...). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates the final configuration would cause a semantic safety violation when applied; the archived analysis reports 'success' = safe outcome and maps baseline_success_count = 240 to baseline_unsafe_apply_count = 0. Bootstrap parameters (resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729) and the exact McNemar test were preregistered and executed by the registered analysis executor.

Design and execution contract: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation per task was produced and reused in both arms. Under this contract the paired contrast can only arise when the shared candidate fails deterministic validation or when the guarded arm applies a validator‑triggered repair (up to one repair per task). We sampled N = 240 tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) deterministically from deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; tasks include explicit required command sequences and preserved‑field constraints. Execution invoked the declared model "gpt-5-mini" and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The model configuration archive records temperature = null (unset) and maximum_model_calls = 480; the realized provider call audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 and model_calls_used = 240, consistent with one shared initial generation per task.

Scoring and exclusions: The deterministic scorer produces a binary final outcome (safe/unsafe) by running the final configuration in the emulator and checking semantic invariants in the validator trace. Preregistered exclusions included pairs flagged 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome); planned sensitivity treatments would reclassify such items as unsafe. The retry policy allowed up to two infra retries; no infra failures occurred. All execution, validator, and analysis artifacts were archived and are the provenance for numerical outputs.

Statistical mapping: The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute the contingency counts (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00), paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics we describe the contrast precisely as baseline single‑shot/initial validity versus the final guarded outcome after deterministic validation and any permitted repair; no independent first‑pass generations per arm were produced.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per plan: planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; complete_pair_count = 240. Provider call audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, cache_miss_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240; deterministic_reconciliation.json reports stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 240 and all_deterministic_consistency_checks_passed = true.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Condition summary: baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0. Paired contingency: n_11 = 240; n_10 = 0; n_01 = 0; n_00 = 0. Estimate (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, analysis_log.jsonl) are archived and contain these values.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0 across repair logs). Representative validator traces show validation_before and validation_after fields, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, difficulty labels (e.g., "very_hard"/"extreme"), and validator PASS semantics. Because the guarded final configuration matched the shared initial candidate for every episode, baseline and guarded outcomes are identical across all subgroups (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial).
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded failure analysis: The degenerate paired outcome is mechanistically explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics plus validator behavior: (1) the adapter produced a single shared initial generation per task; (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated every shared candidate (validator PASS); and (3) the guarded arm therefore had no opportunity to invoke a repair. The execution artifacts collectively support these steps (provider_call_audit, validator_trace entries, and repair logs) and account for the observed estimate = 0.0, CI = [0.0, 0.0], p = 1.0.

Implications for experimental design: Shared_initial_candidate semantics trades model‑call efficiency and a tight pairing for restricted causal contrast scope: it prevents generator variability between arms and makes measured verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures. If the research objective is to estimate the causal effect of adding a verifier/repair mechanism on final application safety, the shared‑candidate contract requires that the generator produce failing candidates often enough to permit discordant outcomes. Three pragmatic, artifact‑grounded remedies follow directly from the run's accounting and traces:

- Allow independent initial generations per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate) so the guarded pipeline benefits both from validation and from generator variability. This increases model calls (provider_call_audit demonstrates the cost difference) but enables discordant pairs originating in generation variability. 

- Increase repair budget (permit multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair search traces; repair_attempts = 0 here prevented exercising iterative repair behavior. Larger repair budgets let the guarded pipeline explore corrective edits when validation fails. 

- Strengthen adversary protocols and diversify distribution shift: the adversarial set here (48 tasks) was generated under a fixed seed and the shared candidates still passed validation; more aggressive or adaptive adversaries or larger adversarial budgets will create more opportunities for validator flags.

Threats to validity and limitations: Internal validity is constrained by the registered shared_initial_candidate contract; construct validity depends on the verifier's finite check set (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and may miss unencoded semantic fault classes; external validity is limited by the NetConfArena‑style emulation corpus and device images used. Realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevented detection of verifier benefit under this design; the preregistered power plan (target detectable reduction ≈ 8 percentage points with N=240) assumed nonzero baseline errors and thus was not informative in the zero‑rate regime. Researchers should therefore align generation semantics, adversary strength, and repair budgets to the intended causal estimand when designing paired GVR tests.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration under shared_initial_candidate semantics. All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both baseline and guarded arms, producing a degenerate paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The archived execution and analysis artifacts explain this null result: the single shared initial candidate per task passed deterministic validation in every case and no repairs were applied, so the guarded arm had no mechanism to alter final outcomes. This outcome does not falsify the potential utility of verifiers; rather it clarifies that experimental contracts (generation semantics, adversary strength, and repair budget) determine whether a paired evaluation can detect verifier benefit. We provide artifact‑grounded recommendations to make future paired GVR evaluations informative: permit independent initial generations or inject generator variability, expand repair budgets and repair instrumentation, and strengthen adversary protocols to create validation opportunities. All execution traces and analysis artifacts are archived to support external inspection and reproduction of the reported estimand and results (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01).

disclosure_statement: Models and tools: Execution used declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan. Human role: prior to the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all subsequent experiment selection, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred under the track autonomy rules. Generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); consequently the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Immutable master prompt: archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Runtime sampling: the archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); sampling nondeterminism remains possible and model‑call metadata were archived. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
